sections.text: Little by little, by the help of his reason controlled by fortitude, let him attain peace; and, fixing his mind on the Self, let him not think of any other thing.
When the volatile and wavering mind would wander, let him restrain it and bring it again to its allegiance to the Self.
Supreme Bliss is the lot of the sage, whose mind attains Peace, whose passions subside, who is without sin, and who becomes one with the Absolute.

Unlike a car with its users manual, we are born without instructions how to live. We experience life vicissitudes without a so called users manual. The Gita has been described as such a guide. So those of you who remember, we were on chapter six two weeks ago and we discussed verses 25, 26, and 27. Chapter six is Dhyana Yoga. The first six chapters, as we have discussed many times, describe the you part of that.
You are That -- Thou art, Tattvamasi -- in the Upanishads. The you part is you and I, who we are. The first six chapters culminate into Dhyana Yoga: who I am, which I cant understand right now, I can reflect on and find through the self. This false notion -- this is me, this body, mind and intellect -- to undo this, I have to contemplate on that self. Once I find myself by myself and become content in myself, then my yoga is complete.
Thats what we have seen. The verse says: Atmanam pashyan atmani tushyati -- seeing the self by the self,
Im satisfied in myself. Thats the goal of life. I want contentment, I want happiness which is everlasting. I looked at, I sought that outside. I finally find in myself. And once I find that in myself, Im satisfied, content.
So the first six chapters told us who we are, what our shortcomings are, and how to overcome them, culminating in meditation. We came across a new definition of yoga in the last few verses: Duhkha samyoga viyoga is yoga -- disassociation from the association with sorrows is yoga. Right now we actually associate with our sorrows, and therefore we are sorrowful. I have an ache and pain in my leg and I think I have pain. I start associating with this pain -- somebody pricks me and thats my pain.
But when a doctor or nurse is ready to give me an injection, Im already prepared for that. I disassociate myself from that pain so I can tolerate it without any problem, because I have already disengaged and said, Thats not really pain, not something unnatural happening to me. That attitude of disassociating yourself from the association with pain -- pain exists, sorrows exist, but my association with that ends. Bhagavan says thats Yoga: Duhkha Samyoga Viyoga.
And therefore Duhkhena guruna api na vichalyate -- even when the greatest sorrows come from the outside world, they seem like the greatest sorrows from my perspective, but those are just the natural occurrences of this world. They happen just as the laws of nature predict. The yogi who has disassociated himself from sorrows is without any disturbance. He has found himself by himself and finds this infinite joy and happiness in that.
The next three verses go along with verse 24: Sankalpa prabhavan kaman tyaktva, manasaivendriyagramam viniyamya samanthatah. You have traveled that journey from ignorance about yourself to understanding whats not right in your internal instrument, the mind and intellect. Purifying it through Karma Yoga, contemplating on that self, I have come to this point: I have given up all the desire-prompted actions, all the desires prompted by the Sankalpa Shakti of my mind. I may have normal desires like Im thirsty and I want water. Thats not Sankalpa Prabhavan Kama -- those are not born out of my fanciful imagination. Im thirsty, so I need water.
But the Sankalpa Shakti in my mind is my mind projects a future, imaginary future and say if I do this then I can do this and then I will have this and then Ill gain this and then Ill be a millionaire. Well thats my Sankalpa Shakti. And what I do is before I start a plan to achieve that goal, my mind has already moved on to another goal. But I can also do this and then do this and then do this and then I can be a billionaire. So before even I start any concrete actions to achieve my goal my mind has erased that goal and gave me another goal. So Im constantly chasing the goal which is not there.
By that time I start working on my goal. My goal has moved away. So Im aimlessly moving. And you see that Sankalpa Shakti. All the desires prompted by this fanciful nature of my mind. When I give up asesata without leaving anything behind.
In other words, I will live in the present, work in the present, and all my goals which are grounded in my life, Ill work towards. Thats not what the Gita says you should give up. It says give up Sankalpa Prabhavan -- all the desires prompted by this fanciful nature of the mind. Manasaivendriyagramam viniyamya -- and then controlling all the senses, which are my instruments to transact with this world outside.
My sense of sight, sound, touch, smell, taste -- I control them by my mind. The senses really do not have any power until the mind plays tricks with them. If I control my mind, my mind is now steady because it is inwardly focused on myself, and I control all the senses through my mind. Then the verse we have seen: Shanaih shanaih uparamet buddhya dhriti grihitaya, atma sanstham manah krutva na kinchid api chintayet.
He says this is not going to come overnight. You have to constantly practice. Then gradually -- Shanaih, gradually -- you will gain control over this through the firm, purified intellect, which has been purified by all the practices we talked about in the first six chapters: selfless actions and so on. And now this purified intellect, this pure intellect, is seeing reality as it is. What is right and what is wrong.
What is really good for me and what is not good for me. With that intellect I. I gradually get the control and get this peace and say Atma Sanstam Manaha Kratva. Mind is established in the self. Its not running outside to fulfilling these fanciful desires. It established in the self. Kincit Apinachintayat Yogi.
Such a seeker will not be thinking about anything but the self. In other words, now I clearly see the difference between I and the instruments of my transaction with the world. This body, mind and intellect are just instruments which I use to transact with this world. That duality only exists in my mind. Myself and your self and his self is one and the same self. This duality has created these sorrows for me.
This Establishment in the self gives me the contentment which I had been seeking for. And now comes the prescription. Because we think that once I have figured out and Im established in meditation, that everything is over. I have now achieved what Im going to achieve. And after that theres not really much efforts left for me. So the next verse, Bhagavan reminds us that this is a constant effort to control your mind.
If you think the mind is going to turn towards yourself and that is the end of the story that is going to remain there, you are mistaken. The very nature of mind is restless. The mind is called mind because it is the flow of thoughts. And a flow of thoughts. Keeping in one direction is going to be difficult. So therefore you need to be vigilant with your intellect, constantly watching what the mind is doing. The very nature of the mind is chanchalam asthiram -- restless, unsteady. You cant think of the one thing for a long period of time. Im thinking about something and suddenly I hear something and my mind just runs away. Im thinking about doing something and my mind sees something and it runs away from that. It is the very nature of the mind to use the senses as its gateways and runs away.
And I say, dont try to punish yourself for that. But remember that your job is to bring that mind back to where it needs to be. So you have to train this mind and tell this mind this is not right. Youre trying to meditate, youre trying to study. Youre trying to do something which you decided is good for you. This is what you want to do.
But hearing something, listening something, seeing something, mind runs away. Dont get discouraged. But bring the mind back and say, you should be doing this right now. So Bhagawan says, yatha yattaha nisharati manaha chanchalam astiram tathaha tathaha niyamya etad atmani evam vasam nayat. Whenever, whenever mind does that. That time you bring the mind and establish back into yourself by yourself.
Bring your mind, turn it towards yourself and then say prasantamanasamhinam yoginam sukhamuttamam. Why are we doing all of that? Why do you want to control the mind? Just because I want to punish my mind, say no, no. What youre looking for was happiness, Sukham. You are looking for a happiness which is everlasting.
Therefore its uttamam, not the regular ones which we get for a While and then it goes away. Well, we had been good. We had been going through this all our life and we are not very happy about it. We want something everlasting. Give me something which I never have to return back to the. I want something permanent happiness.
Bhagawan said the only permanent happiness comes from Prasantamanah. By a quiet mind is the only source of joy and happiness. Agitated mind cannot give you any happiness. I may be telling you the greatest news of your life. But if your mind is agitated, you wont listen to me. I may be giving you the greatest gift you can receive.
But if your mind is agitated, you wont even see it. So it is the mind which decides whether I am happy or not. So what is the quality of the mind which is in happiness? The mind which is quiet gives me happiness. And there is a Prasantamanasam Hienam Yoginam Sukha Muttamam. The yogi who has been striving and seeking the self.
Once he finds his self established the mind in it, his mind now becomes quiet. This quietness in the mind gives the Sukham Uttamam the greatest happiness. Sensing Upeti Santa Rajasam. You know why he gets the happiness? Shanta Rajasam Rajasa activity. You know this Sattva Rajasantamas the very nature of the mind is to be Rajasa want to run away.
When you make this mind quiet out of his habit of running away into say stay quiet. You know it gives the happiness. Brahma Bhutam Akalpasham with this practice of meditation when I purified my mind and intellect. Now I have trained my mind to be steady which is contrary to its own nature of running away. This quiet mind removes all my sin or kalmasam and the Yogi becomes without any sin. And the sin is nothing but the impurities in my internal instruments mind and intellect.
Im purified by those impurities. I now realize that myself and the supreme self is one and the same self. So I become Brahma Bhutam. Ive now identified myself with the eternal self which is all pervading, an almighty and omniscient and omnipotent. Then in my previous case I identified myself with this limited self which is limit in my body. A limit of my mental capacity and my intellectual capacity.
All my problems are because my identification with this limitedness. Now because I have now identified myself with the supreme. All my problems have dissolved into a permanent peace.

The word shanaih shanaih - gradually, gradually - in verse 25 offers tremendous encouragement. This is not a path of sudden transformation but patient cultivation. With a pure intellect (buddhya dhriti-grihitaya), you gradually withdraw the mind from its outward rushing and establish it in the self. The key is not to expect overnight results, but to trust the process and continue. Like learning to drive a car - initially overwhelming, eventually automatic - the practice of steadying the mind becomes natural through repetition.
Verse 26 acknowledges reality with compassion: Yato yato nishcharati manash chanchalam asthiram - wherever and whenever the restless, unsteady mind wanders, bring it back. This is not a verse of condemnation but of practical instruction. The mind WILL wander - that is its nature. Your job is not to prevent wandering but to notice it and return. Each return strengthens the faculty of awareness. Dont punish yourself for wandering; celebrate each return. You are training a wild horse, and every gentle redirection is progress.
The reward described in verse 27 is the purpose behind all this effort: Prasanta-manasam hy enam yoginam sukham uttamam - supreme bliss comes to the yogi whose mind is peaceful, whose rajas (restlessness) is subdued, who has become one with Brahman and is free from sin. The sins mentioned are the impurities of the internal instrument - the vasanas and tendencies that drive us toward wrong action. When these are purified through meditation, the yogi realizes that the individual self and the Supreme Self were always one. Today, practice this: when your mind wanders during any activity, gently whisper return and bring attention back. Do this ten times and notice how the quality of your experience changes.
